A content delivery network is a system of computer servers spread across many locations worldwide, working together to deliver websites and videos faster. Normally, every request for a webpage travels all the way to one central computer called the origin server, which is where the website's original files live. If many people in different countries request that page at once, the trip back and forth can feel slow, especially for someone far from that central computer. To fix this, copies of the website's files get stored on servers placed closer to people, called edge locations, since they sit at the "edge" of the network, nearer everyday visitors. When someone requests a page and a nearby edge location already has a saved copy ready to serve, that's called a cache hit, meaning the answer arrives quickly without bothering the distant origin server at all. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries holding copies of a popular book instead of everyone traveling to one faraway national archive. This setup reduces delays, spreads out heavy traffic, and keeps websites running smoothly even during busy periods or sudden spikes in visitors. Streaming services, online stores, and news sites all rely on this approach to keep pages loading quickly worldwide.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|------|---------------|-----------------|
| Origin server | The original computer storing a website's true files | Everything ultimately comes from here if no copy exists nearby |
| Edge location | A server placed close to everyday visitors | Shortens the distance information must travel |
| Cache hit | A request answered instantly from a nearby saved copy | Speeds up loading and reduces strain on the origin |
| Latency | The delay between requesting and receiving information | Lower delay means a smoother, faster browsing experience |
